question.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Whose Denominator Contains a Leading Coefficient
question.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $4$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{4x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{4(x-\frac{1}{4})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{(x-\frac{1}{4})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{1}{4} & 8 & 1 \\  & ↓ & 2 \\  & 8 & 3\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8x+1}{(x-\frac{1}{4})} & =8+\frac{3}{(x-\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =8+\frac{12}{4x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{4x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}(8+\frac{12}{4x-1})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\text{d}x+12{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{1}{4x-1}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8x+3\operatorname{ln}⁡|4x-1|]_{-1/8}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8(0-(-\frac{1}{8}))+3(\operatorname{ln}⁡|4(0)-1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|4(-\frac{1}{8})-1|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8(\frac{1}{8})+3(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2}))] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[1-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2})].\end{aligned}
$$

judgment.reasoning:
All 16 selected answers agree with their own captured worked solutions and are mathematically correct. There are authored errors in the explanations: q-49354 changes the denominator from x+2 to x+5 in one displayed integral, although its decomposition and final answer correctly use x+2. In q-2751 and q-79342, the source incorrectly says the derivatives are undefined at the endpoints; the displayed functions have derivatives there. Endpoints are extrema candidates regardless of whether they are interior critical points. These errors do not change the answers.

For q-77888, only h is continuous on [-1,3] and differentiable on (-1,3). The other graphs have a discontinuity, an interior corner, or an endpoint asymptote. For q-48399, f's discontinuity at -1 is outside [0,2], and its graph is smooth throughout (0,2); the other choices fail continuity or differentiability. For q-127013, II and III have their corners at endpoints, while I has an interior corner. For q-125262, I and III are smooth everywhere; ln(x) is undefined at 0.

For q-12497, u=3x+1 produces (1/9)∫(u^(3/2)-u^(1/2))du. For q-2621, u=4-x produces -∫(9u^(1/2)-2u^(3/2))du. For q-49529, x=(u+1)/2 and dx=du/2, with bounds 1 and 5, give the factor 1/4. For q-17045, u=2-x gives ∫₀²(2-u)u^(3/2)du=32√2/35=√(2^11)/35.

The rational integrands in q-49354, q-49456, and q-73392 decompose respectively as 5-3/(x+2), 3x²+1+2/(x-3), and 1/2-2/(x+3), yielding the stated antiderivatives. For q-114898, the integrand is 2+3/(4x-1); evaluating 2x+(3/4)ln|4x-1| gives [1-3ln(3/2)]/4.

For q-4798, reversing and scaling the given integral gives ∫₃⁶f=5, so ∫₀⁶f=3+5=8. For q-114019, ∫₋₁¹f=1 and the odd term -6x integrates to zero. For q-2751, √x increases, so its maximum is √9=3. For q-79342, the endpoint and stationary-point values at -1,0,2,3 are 3,-1,3,-1, so the minimum is -1. There is no earlier submitted answer or revealed grade to reconcile.
